title: Rolling PCM window uses Array.removeFirst — O(n) memmove on every far-end audio callback once the 10-min cap is hit
description: CapturedAudio's drop-oldest loop calls buffers.removeFirst(), which shifts the whole array. With bufferSeconds=600 at 16 kHz and ~171-frame converted buffers, the array holds ~56,000 entries at cap; from minute 10 of a multilingual meeting onward, EVERY IOProc callback (~94x/sec) memmoves ~450 KB of pointers (~42 MB/s sustained) inside the audio I/O queue's lock, for the rest of the meeting. AudioCapture.swift:33-36 has the identical pattern (much smaller: ~7k entries for the mic path). Cheap to fix, pure waste to keep.
evidence: while totalFrames > maxFrames, let first = buffers.first { totalFrames -= AVAudioFramePosition(first.frameLength); buffers.removeFirst() }
proposed_fix: Replace the Array with a head-index ring: keep `var head = 0`, advance head instead of removeFirst, and compact (buffers.removeFirst(head); head = 0) only when head exceeds e.g. half the capacity — or use Deque from swift-collections if the dependency is acceptable. Apply the same change to the identical private CapturedAudio in AudioCapture.swift.

title: Meeting partial flush re-renders the whole transcript, JSON-encodes, and writes to disk on the main actor
description: flushPartialIfDirty (called from the 1 Hz tick) rebuilds the ENTIRE transcript via MeetingTranscriptRenderer.render(turns) — an O(n log n) sort plus full string join over all turns — then JSON-encodes and synchronously writes the file, all on the main actor. The dirty check helps at idle, but during active conversation the turn count changes every few seconds, and while the user types live notes the `notes` comparison makes it dirty EVERY second — each time re-rendering a transcript that hasn't changed. At 2 hours that's a ~100 KB render+encode+atomic write per second on the UI thread while the user is typing.
evidence: transcript: MeetingTranscriptRenderer.render(turns) ... try? data.write(to: partialURL, options: .atomic)
proposed_fix: Cache the rendered transcript keyed by the turn count (re-render only when lastFlushedTurnCount changes, reuse the cached string when only notes/farEnd changed), and move the encode+write off the main actor: snapshot the RecordingPartial value and perform Self.encodePartial + data.write on a detached utility task or a dedicated serial queue (the write is already atomic, so ordering per-flush is enough).

title: Per-callback allocations in both audio capture callbacks (fresh AVAudioPCMBuffer + SingleShotInput per buffer)
description: The far-end IOProc (~94x/sec for the whole meeting) allocates per callback: an AVAudioPCMBuffer wrapper via bufferListNoCopy (line 278), a SingleShotInput object, and a fresh output AVAudioPCMBuffer in convert() (line 539) sized ratio*frames+1024. The mic tap does the same at ~12x/sec (AudioCapture.swift:223-242, output alloc at 372). That's ~200+ transient ObjC/audio-buffer allocations per second sustained for hours during meetings — steady allocator churn on audio-delivery threads. Note: the doc comment on MeetingAudioFileWriter.append says the copy-free tee RELIES on a fresh output buffer per convert, so a single reused buffer is NOT safe here.
evidence: guard let output = AVAudioPCMBuffer(pcmFormat: targetFormat, frameCapacity: capacity) else { return nil }
proposed_fix: Introduce a small fixed-size pool (e.g. 4-8 preallocated output buffers recycled round-robin, sized for the max callback length) captured by value into the tap/IOProc block, instead of allocating per callback; keep pool size > the tee writer's queue depth so the no-alias contract holds, or have MeetingAudioFileWriter copy the buffer at enqueue time (one memcpy of ~11 KB, cheaper than an allocation) and then a single reused conversion buffer suffices. Reuse one SingleShotInput per converter by making it resettable.

title: ActiveMeetingDetector polls Core Audio every 1.5s forever — all-day timer wake-ups that could be event-driven
description: The detector loop (startLoop, lines 241-250 / pollOnce line 273) wakes every 1.5 seconds for the app's entire lifetime, enumerating every audio process object and issuing 2-3 AudioObjectGetPropertyData IPC reads per process (kAudioProcessPropertyPID / BundleID / IsRunningInput) plus array allocations per poll. For an always-running menu-bar app this is ~57,600 wake-ups/day of idle work and defeats timer coalescing/App Nap even when no meeting app is running.
evidence: var pollInterval: Duration = .seconds(1.5)
proposed_fix: Make it event-driven: register AudioObjectAddPropertyListenerBlock on kAudioObjectSystemObject for kAudioHardwarePropertyProcessObjectList (process set changes) and on each process object for kAudioProcessPropertyIsRunningInput; run the existing bestCandidate/decide state machine only on those callbacks plus a slow (e.g. 30s) safety-net tick for the end-debounce. Falls back to the current poll if listener registration fails.

title: CleanupEngine.generate re-runs NLLanguageRecognizer on the same strings up to twice each, per segment, on the insert-critical path
description: dominantLanguageCode(trimmed) is computed at line 225 (when languageCode is nil) and recomputed verbatim at line 263; dominantLanguageCode(cleaned) is computed at line 264 and recomputed at line 274. Each call constructs a fresh NLLanguageRecognizer and re-processes the full string (LanguageDetector.swift:81-87). This runs per finalized segment inside the cleanup await that the final paste waits on — 2 redundant detector passes (~ms each on long segments) added to hotkey-to-insert latency for zero benefit.
evidence: let inCode = LanguageDetector.dominantLanguageCode(trimmed), let outCode = LanguageDetector.dominantLanguageCode(cleaned)
proposed_fix: Compute `let inCode = pinnedCode ?? LanguageDetector.dominantLanguageCode(trimmed)` and `let outCode = LanguageDetector.dominantLanguageCode(cleaned)` once each into locals before the guard chain, and reuse those locals in both the translation guard (lines 261-268) and the pinned-language guard (lines 272-277). No behavior change: the same values feed the same comparisons.

title: Analyzer input streams use unbounded AsyncStream buffering — a stalled consumer accumulates PCM without bound in long meetings
description: AsyncStream<AnalyzerInput>.makeStream() defaults to .unbounded buffering here, in MultiLangStreamTranscriber (lines 166 and 194 — the fanout input and every per-lane stream), and in the re-transcribe path. Converted 16 kHz mono PCM arrives at ~64 KB/s per stream; the codebase itself documents that a long-lived SpeechAnalyzer can stall (~30 min in). If a stall (or a wedged lane after a failed rotation) ever slows consumption rather than just finalization, buffered AnalyzerInputs grow at ~230 MB/hour per affected stream with no backpressure and no visibility.
evidence: let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream<AnalyzerInput>.makeStream()
proposed_fix: Use makeStream(bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(N)) with N sized to a few seconds of audio (e.g. 512 buffers) for the live session and lane streams — dropping the oldest audio under a wedged consumer is strictly better than unbounded memory growth — or at minimum add a yield-result check / periodic depth log so a stalled lane is detectable. Keep .unbounded only for the finite re-transcribe replay where the producer completes immediately.

title: LatencyStore encodes and writes latency.json synchronously on the main actor after every dictation
description: record() → save() JSON-encodes up to 50 records and does a synchronous atomic file write on the @MainActor, once per completed dictation. It runs after insertion so it doesn't add to felt hotkey-to-text latency, but it is recurring main-thread file I/O (plus the @Published records mutation triggering SwiftUI diffing) at the exact moment the user resumes interacting with their app.
evidence: guard let data = try? JSONEncoder().encode(records) else { return } try? data.write(to: fileURL, options: .atomic)
proposed_fix: Snapshot `records` into a local and perform the encode+write in a detached background task (Task.detached(priority: .utility)) or a serial queue; writes are idempotent full-file snapshots so last-writer-wins ordering on a serial queue is sufficient.

title: MeetingsView rebuilds every meeting row (word-counting full transcripts) once per second while recording and on every notes keystroke
description: The meeting list is a plain `VStack` (line 50) with `ForEach(store.meetings)` (line 72) — NOT a LazyVStack — so all meetings (MeetingStore caps at 200) are built eagerly. Each `MeetingRow` body does `WordCounter.count(meeting.transcript)` (line 581), an O(transcript-length) whitespace split over the FULL transcript, plus a `MarkdownText` parse of the whole summary (line 632, and MarkdownText.parsedLines re-parses on every body pass). MeetingsView is `@ObservedObject var recorder` and reads `recorder.elapsed` (line 202), which is `@Published` and ticked by a 1 s Timer in MeetingRecorder.swift:461; the live-notes editor binds `$recorder.notes` (line 251), publishing on every keystroke. Because MeetingRow carries closures (onReveal/onCopy/…), SwiftUI cannot prove row equality and re-runs every row body. Net: with 200 meetings at ~30–60 KB transcript each, every recording-second and every notes keystroke re-splits ~5–10 MB of strings and re-parses 200 markdown summaries on the main thread — visible keystroke lag exactly when a meeting is live.
evidence: Text("\(Int((meeting.durationSec / 60).rounded())) min · \(WordCounter.count(meeting.transcript)) words")
proposed_fix: 1) Change the meetings list container to `LazyVStack`. 2) Cache the word count (compute once in `Meeting` at save time or memoize per row via a `let` computed at init from an Equatable wrapper). 3) Move the elapsed readout into a tiny child view (e.g. `RecordingElapsedText(recorder:)`) so only it observes the 1 Hz tick, and give the notes editor a local @State draft committed on debounce/blur instead of binding `$recorder.notes` directly. 4) Make MeetingRow conform to Equatable on (meeting, expanded inputs) and add `.equatable()` so unchanged rows skip body re-evaluation.

title: Memory search runs the full semantic scan synchronously on the main thread on every keystroke, with no debounce
description: `searchResults` calls `searchEngine.search(trimmedQuery)` directly inside the view body, and `query` is a plain `@State` bound to the TextField — so every keystroke re-evaluates the body and runs `SemanticIndex.search` (SemanticIndex.swift:267) synchronously on the main actor. That search embeds the query via NLEmbedding and computes cosine similarity over EVERY indexed chunk: up to 2000 dictations + 200 meetings × up to 80 chunks each (TranscriptChunker.maxChunks = 80) + 2000 graph entities — potentially ~10–20k cosine ops over 512-dim Double vectors per keystroke (tens of millions of multiply-adds), plus an NLEmbedding vector lookup. With a large corpus this is easily 50–200 ms per keystroke of main-thread work, i.e. typing lag in the Memory tab. The body also re-runs the search when any observed store publishes (contextGraph, history, searchEngine.recordCount).
evidence: let hits = searchEngine.search(trimmedQuery)
proposed_fix: Debounce the query (~150–250 ms) and run the search off the main actor: store `@State private var hits: [SearchHit]` and drive it from `.task(id: trimmedQuery)` that sleeps for the debounce, then calls a `nonisolated`/detached search over the Sendable SemanticIndex (it already is Sendable) and assigns results back on the main actor. Body then renders the cached `hits` instead of searching inline.

title: MeetingStore.save() JSON-encodes all 200 retained meetings — full transcripts and timed segments inline — synchronously on the main actor
description: meetings.json inlines full data for up to `maxRetainedMeetings = 200` meetings (line 420), where each `Meeting` carries `transcript`, `summary`, AND `segments: [MeetingSegment]?` (per-utterance text + timings — roughly doubling the transcript bytes). A 1-hour meeting is ~50–150 KB in the index, so the file can reach 10–30 MB. `save()` (lines 674–677) does `JSONEncoder().encode(meetings)` + atomic write synchronously on the main actor, and it runs on every `add`, `update` (summary regen, transcript edit), `retitle`, `restoreTitle`, and `delete` — a hundreds-of-ms UI hitch at exactly the moments the user is interacting (meeting just ended, saving an edit). `load()` (line 587) pays the same decode cost on the main thread at process start (see the startup finding).
proposed_fix: Adopt the exact pattern HistoryStore already uses (HistoryStore.swift:36 `actor HistoryFileWriter` + generation-tokened debounced save): snapshot `meetings` (value type, Sendable), hand it to a `MeetingIndexWriter` actor that encodes + writes off-main, with a monotonic generation so stale writes drop. No format change needed; callers stay synchronous.

title: All ~19 stores synchronously read + JSON-decode their files on the main thread before the first frame
description: main.swift:35 constructs `AppDelegate()` before `app.run()`, and AppDelegate declares ~19 stores as eagerly-initialized stored properties (lines 11–68: settings, dictionary, history, stats, appUsage, activity, wordFreq, jobTitle, latency, scratchpad, profileImage, autoAddPreviewLog, projectIndex, contextSummary, meetingStore, contextGraph, macros, profiles, searchEngine, nicheVocab). Every one calls `load()` in its init — a synchronous `Data(contentsOf:)` + `JSONDecoder` on the main thread. The heavy ones: history.json (up to 2000 full-text entries, ~0.5–2 MB), meetings.json (200 meetings with inline transcripts + segments, potentially 10–30 MB), entities.json (2000 entities × 12 provenance snippets each, ~1–5 MB, plus a prune pass), profile.png decode. Launch is blocked on this serial disk + decode chain before the menu-bar item or window can appear.
evidence: let history = HistoryStore() … let meetingStore = MeetingStore() … let contextGraph = ContextGraphStore()  (all `load()` in init; main.swift: `let delegate = AppDelegate()`)
proposed_fix: Stage the loads: keep tiny stores (settings, stats, activity, appUsage, latency, macros, profiles) eager, and make the big three (HistoryStore, MeetingStore, ContextGraphStore) load off-main — init with empty state, kick a `Task.detached` that reads + decodes, then applies on the main actor (each store already isolates mutation behind private(set) @Published, so an `apply(loaded:)` method suffices). Dashboard/Meetings views already handle empty state gracefully. Alternatively lazy-load MeetingStore/ContextGraph on first tab visit / first ingest.

title: MainView observes ~18 stores it never reads — any @Published change anywhere re-evaluates the entire window body
description: MainView (the window root) declares `@ObservedObject` for essentially every store (lines 206–237: history, stats, appUsage, activity, wordFreq, jobTitle, latency, systemPressure, scratchpad, profileImage, projectIndex, contextSummary, meetingRecorder, meetingStore, contextGraph, macros, profiles, searchEngine, nicheVocab…), but its body only reads `settings.hasOnboarded` and `router.selectedTab` — everything else is pass-through to child views that observe on their own. Consequence: every publish anywhere (each of StatsStore's ~6 @Published mutations per dictation, history entries, contextGraph entities, searchEngine.recordCount, and notably MeetingRecorder.elapsed ticking at 1 Hz for the whole duration of any recording — MeetingRecorder.swift:95/461) invalidates the whole NavigationSplitView + active tab body. Combined with the closure-carrying child views (which defeat SwiftUI's equality skip), this makes the entire window re-render once per second during recordings and several times per dictation-end, even when the visible tab shows none of that data. The file's own comment on line 225 shows the team knows the right pattern (autoAddPreviewLog is a plain `let` because "nothing here should redraw when it changes").
evidence: @ObservedObject var meetingRecorder: MeetingRecorder … // Not `@ObservedObject` — this log drives no UI, so nothing here should redraw when it changes.
proposed_fix: Change every pass-through store on MainView (and the same pattern on MainWindowController) from `@ObservedObject var` to plain `let` — keep `@ObservedObject` only for `settings` and `router`, which the body actually reads. Child views (DashboardView cards, MeetingsView, MemoryView) already observe what they render.

title: ContextGraphStore.save() re-encodes the whole 2000-entity graph synchronously on the main actor after every dictation
description: `ingest()` (lines 59–63) runs at the end of every dictation (AppDelegate.swift:2198) and calls `save()`, which JSON-encodes `Array(entities.values)` — up to `entityCap = 2000` entities, each carrying up to 12 provenance records with 120-char snippets (~1–5 MB of JSON) — plus a second encode+write for the watermark file, all synchronously on the main actor (the class is @MainActor). This lands in the same main-actor turn as the HUD finishing, text insertion, and 5+ other store saves, adding tens of ms of encode+I/O to the dictation hot path. The store's own comment admits the tradeoff: the cap keeps the file 'small enough to load and re-encode in full on every save()' — but per-dictation full rewrites on the UI actor is the one place that assumption hurts.
evidence:
if let data = try? JSONEncoder().encode(Array(entities.values)) {
            try? data.write(to: fileURL, options: .atomic)
proposed_fix: Reuse the HistoryFileWriter pattern (HistoryStore.swift:36): snapshot `Array(entities.values)` (Entity is Codable/Sendable value data) and hand it plus a generation token to a writer actor that debounces ~250 ms and encodes + writes off-main. The watermark write can ride the same actor.

title: Context-graph backfill mines phrases over the entire history + all meeting transcripts on the main actor at launch
description: In applicationDidFinishLaunching, `Task { @MainActor in contextGraph.backfill(dictations: history.entries, meetings: meetingStore.meetings) … }` (lines 405–426) runs the backfill ON the main actor. `backfill` (ContextGraphStore.swift:98–127) runs `ContextGraphExtractor.candidates(from:)` — PhraseMiner over the full text — for every dictation and every meeting transcript past the watermark, then a full `save()`. The watermark makes steady-state launches cheap, but the FIRST launch (fresh watermark file, reinstall, or restored support dir) processes up to 2000 dictations plus 200 full meeting transcripts (~10 MB of text through PhraseMiner) in one uninterruptible main-actor turn right as the UI comes up — a multi-second beachball on exactly the launch where the user is forming a first impression. The extractor is documented 'Pure + Sendable; safe to run off the main actor' but is not run off it.
evidence:
Task { @MainActor in
            contextGraph.backfill(dictations: history.entries, meetings: meetingStore.meetings)
proposed_fix: Split backfill: compute candidates off-main (`ContextGraphExtractor.candidates` is already pure/Sendable — run the per-source extraction in a `Task.detached(priority: .utility)` over value-type snapshots of entries/meetings), then hop to the main actor only for the `upsert` fold + one save. Alternatively chunk the main-actor work with `await Task.yield()` between sources.

title: Every dictation triggers a full search-index rebuild — re-chunking, re-hashing and re-tokenizing the entire corpus and rewriting the whole vector sidecar
description: AppDelegate.swift:413–425 merges history/meetings/graph publishers into `scheduleRebuild`, so each dictation (which changes all three) schedules a full rebuild. The 200 ms debounce and off-main detached build are good, but the rebuild itself is O(corpus), not O(delta): it loads the entire sidecar into a `[String: [Double]]` (every 512-dim vector widened Float32→Double: ~8–15k chunks ≈ 30–60 MB transient), re-runs TranscriptChunker + `SemanticIndex.tokenize` over every record, rebuilds all Entry structs, and rewrites the full vectors.bin/ids/meta set to disk — per dictation, all day. The resulting SemanticIndex also permanently holds every chunk's `[Double]` vector + token Set in memory on the main actor (~30–60 MB resident for a full corpus). Embedding reuse via the hash cache is the only incremental part.
evidence:
func scheduleRebuild(dictations: [DictationEntry], meetings: [Meeting], graph: ContextGraphSnapshot) {
        rebuildTask?.cancel()
proposed_fix: Two cheap wins without changing the architecture: (1) store vectors as `[Float]` end-to-end (halves resident + transient memory; cosine in Float is fine for ranking); (2) make dictation-append incremental — keep the previous SemanticIndex and add/remove entries for changed record ids instead of rebuilding, falling back to full rebuild only for meetings/graph churn or on a periodic timer. Also lengthen the debounce for rebuilds triggered by graph-only changes.

title: LiveBackground runs two 30 fps TimelineViews (full-window image transform + three ~100 px-blur glows) the entire time the dashboard is visible
description: Backdrop (line 67) and DriftingGlow (line 121) each run `TimelineView(.animation(minimumInterval: 1.0/30.0))`. Every tick re-renders the full-window wallpaper Image with new `scaleEffect`/`offset`, and composites 3 radial-gradient circles sized up to `1.05 × min(w,h)` with `blur(radius: d * 0.16)` (≈ 100+ px blur at window size) under `.plusLighter` — a sustained GPU/compositor load at 30 Hz for as long as the dashboard tab is open and Talkie is active (an all-day-open dashboard is a plausible usage). Pausing is only wired to app-level `didResignActiveNotification` (lines 49–53): the animation does NOT pause when the window is occluded by another of the user's windows/spaces while Talkie technically stays active, nor does it drop rate when nothing changed perceptibly (±12 px over ~100 s does not need 30 fps). Mitigations for Reduce Motion and app-inactive are already correct.
evidence: TimelineView(.animation(minimumInterval: 1.0 / 30.0, paused: !animate)) { ctx in
proposed_fix: Keep the aesthetic; cut the duty cycle: (1) lower `minimumInterval` to ~1/10 s — the drift is ±12 px over ~100 s and 1.5% scale over ~200 s, so 10 fps is visually identical; (2) also gate `active` on window occlusion (`NSWindow.didChangeOcclusionStateNotification` → pause when `!occlusionState.contains(.visible)`); (3) render the three glow circles once into a cached image/layer and animate only its position instead of re-blurring per frame.

title: Heatmap rebuilt with fresh UUID identities for all ~180 cells on every layout pass
description: StreakCard calls `activity.heatmap(weeks: weeks)` inside a GeometryReader closure, so it recomputes on every body evaluation AND every layout pass (window resize drags recompute continuously). `heatmap` (ActivityStore.swift:181) allocates a new `DateFormatter` per call (line 196) and builds up to 26×7 = 182 `HeatCell`s where `let id = UUID()` (ActivityStore.swift:13) — every cell gets a brand-new identity each time, so the `ForEach(week)` in Heatmap treats all 182 cells as removed+inserted rather than diffing them. Combined with the MainView/dashboard-wide invalidations from other findings (per-dictation, per-second-while-recording), this is repeated wasted view churn.
evidence:
struct HeatCell: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
proposed_fix: Give HeatCell a stable identity: `var id: String { date.map { String($0.timeIntervalSinceReferenceDate) } ?? "pad-\(offset)" }` (or key by day index), hoist the DateFormatter to a static, and memoize the HeatmapData by (weeks, activity.days-version) — e.g. compute it in `onChange(of:)`/a cached property instead of inside GeometryReader.

title: Meeting playback ticker fires at 12.5 Hz whenever the transcript is expanded (even paused) and re-renders every segment row while playing
description: MeetingPlaybackView creates `Timer.publish(every: 0.08, on: .main, in: .common).autoconnect()` and subscribes via `.onReceive` (line 920). The timer wakes the main runloop 12.5×/s for as long as the expanded transcript is on screen — including when nothing is playing (tick() guards to a no-op, but the timer still fires; the comment 'it only does work while something is actually playing' is only half true). While playing, each tick sets `currentTime` (@State), re-evaluating the body's `ForEach` over ALL segments — an hour-long meeting has hundreds of `segmentRow`s rebuilt 12.5×/s, when only the previously-active and newly-active rows change.
evidence: private let ticker = Timer.publish(every: 0.08, on: .main, in: .common).autoconnect()
proposed_fix: Store `activeIndex` (an Int?) as the @State instead of raw `currentTime`, and only assign when it actually changed (compute `Meeting.activeSegmentIndex` in tick() and compare) — body then re-renders only on segment transitions (~every few seconds), not per tick. Start/stop the timer with playback: replace the always-on publisher with a Task-based loop launched in `toggle()` and cancelled on pause/disappear.

title: Dictation-end fans out 6+ separate synchronous whole-file JSON writes on the main actor
description: One dictation completion (lines 2162–2200) triggers, in a single main-actor turn: `stats.record` → save, `stats.recordFixes` → save, `stats.recordTermFixes` → save (three full rewrites of stats.json, StatsStore.swift:256), `activity.recordAndCheckBiggestDay` → save (ActivityStore.swift:257), `wordFreq.record` → save with a full sort-based cap pass (WordFrequencyStore.swift:233), `appUsage.record` → save (AppUsageStore.swift:148), plus the ContextGraph save covered separately. Each file is individually small (KB-scale; wordfreq up to ~600 entries), so no single write hurts — but 6–8 encode+atomic-write syscalls on the UI actor sit on the latency-sensitive path between key-release and paste, and HistoryStore in the same codebase already demonstrates the debounced off-main pattern these could share.
evidence:
var brokenRecords = self.stats.record(words: words, durationSec: duration)
            self.stats.recordFixes(
proposed_fix: Lowest-cost: have StatsStore coalesce its three per-dictation saves into one (record/recordFixes/recordTermFixes set a dirty flag; a single deferred save at end of turn via `Task { @MainActor in … }` or an explicit `flushAfterDictation()` call). Optionally generalize HistoryFileWriter into a shared `DebouncedJSONWriter` actor and adopt it in Stats/Activity/AppUsage/WordFrequency stores.

description: Owner-requested removal of the bulk-destructive 'Clear everything' control. The control is a two-step UI in MemoryView: a header 'Clear' trash button (lines 95-100) sets showingClearConfirm, which presents a confirmationDialog (lines 70-76) whose destructive button 'Clear everything' (line 72) runs clearEverything() (lines 129-149), a 9-store cascade: history.clearAll(), contextGraph.purge(source: .dictation, sourceID: nil), wordFreq.clearAll(), jobTitle?.clearCache(), scratchpad.purgeAllDictationSourced(), autoAddPreviewLog?.purgeAllDictationSourced(), contextSummary?.clearSummary(), searchEngine.clearSidecar(), profileImage?.clear(). No factory-reset, no 'clear all meetings', no destructive control in Settings or the Privacy pane.

title: Release builds write full dictation transcripts and other apps' field text to world-readable, predictable /tmp/talkie-lang.log
description: talkieDebugLog() (TranscriptionEngine.swift:8-18) appends to the fixed path /tmp/talkie-lang.log with no #if DEBUG gate and no Dev.isEnabled gate, so it ships in every release build. Files created there get default umask perms (0644) in the world-readable shared /tmp, and the path is predictable — another local user can pre-create the file (or a symlink) and harvest everything appended. What gets written is the user's actual speech: CleanupEngine.swift:279 logs the full raw and cleaned transcript ("cleanup[…]: in='\(trimmed)' out='\(cleaned)'"); OutputTranslator.swift:196 logs full input/output text; TranscriptionEngine.swift:339 logs re-transcription text plus per-word confidences; LearningEngine.swift:88/107 logs learned corrections ('from' → 'to', verbatim user words); and LearningEngine.swift:66 auto-triggers AXFieldReader.logFocusedTree() (AXFieldReader.swift:115), which dumps the focused app's AX tree including 28-char value snippets of OTHER apps' UI fields. The log also grows unbounded (never rotated or shredded, and it survives 'Clear everything'). This directly contradicts the brand promise and the FileShredder/BugBundle care taken elsewhere — BugBundle.swift even acknowledges the file 'records LEARNED corrections that embed the user's actual dictated words' and carefully redacts it for bug reports, while the raw file sits world-readable in /tmp.
evidence: let url = URL(fileURLWithPath: "/tmp/talkie-lang.log")  …  talkieDebugLog("cleanup[\(pinnedCode ?? "?")]: in='\(trimmed)' out='\(cleaned)'")
proposed_fix: In talkieDebugLog (Sources/Talkie/TranscriptionEngine.swift:8-18): (1) guard the entire body with `guard Dev.isEnabled else { return }` (Sources/Talkie/DevTools.swift already provides the flag) so release builds write nothing; (2) move the file from /tmp to AppPaths.supportDirectory().appendingPathComponent("debug.log") and create it with [.posixPermissions: 0o600] via FileManager.createFile before first append (kills both the world-readable and the predictable-path/symlink issues); (3) update BugBundle.debugLogPath (Sources/Talkie/BugBundle.swift:205) to the new location; (4) add the log file to the delete cascade or truncate it on history clear, and cap its size (e.g. truncate at 1 MB). Independently, even in dev mode stop logging full transcript bodies: trim CleanupEngine.swift:279 and OutputTranslator.swift:196 to lengths/language codes only, and TranscriptionEngine.swift:339 to confidence stats without text.

title: Dev updater verifies size/SHA-256 over HTTPS but performs no code-signature check and fails open when a release omits the digest
description: SPECIAL TASK 2 verdict. What's good: all traffic is HTTPS to api.github.com (GitHubReleases.swift:153/168) or via the gh CLI; the Authorization header is stripped on cross-host redirect (RedirectAuthStripper, :253); the token lives in the Keychain (Keychain.swift, kSecClassGenericPassword, never UserDefaults); first network touch is behind an explicit fail-closed consent gate (UpdaterSupport.swift UpdaterConsent); asset byte-size is enforced ALWAYS and SHA-256 fail-closed when present, both checked BEFORE unzip/de-quarantine (UpdateInstaller.performInstall:70-78); release_dev.sh:85-95 computes and publishes the digest. The weaknesses: (1) SHA-256 is enforced only `when expectedSHA256 is present` (UpdateInstaller.swift:52, GitHubReleases.swift:19 'nil for older releases') — a release published WITHOUT a sha256: line installs on the size gate alone, so anyone with repo release-write access can push an undigested artifact that installs; (2) the digest is parsed from the release body (GitHubReleases.sha256(fromBody:), :224), i.e. the same trust domain as the artifact — it proves transfer integrity, not publisher authenticity; (3) before replacing the running app the installer validates only that an executable exists and CFBundleIdentifier == "com.coralate.talkie" (UpdateInstaller.swift:94-100) — no codesign verification, no Team-ID/signing-identity pinning — then strips quarantine (xattr -dr, :106) and swaps the bundle (swap.sh, :123-146). A compromised GitHub account/token = arbitrary code execution on every collaborator's Mac at next update.
evidence: if let expected = expectedSHA256?.lowercased() { … } // SHA-256 is enforced fail-closed ONLY when `expectedSHA256` is present
proposed_fix: (1) Make the digest mandatory going forward: in ReleaseFetcher.pickLatestDev (GitHubReleases.swift:197) skip (or in UpdateInstaller.verifyArtifact reject) any dev release whose body lacks a valid sha256: line — every release since release_dev.sh started publishing digests carries one, so nothing bricks. (2) Add a code-signature gate in performInstall after unzip and BEFORE the xattr de-quarantine at UpdateInstaller.swift:106: run `/usr/bin/codesign --verify --deep --strict <newApp>` via the existing Shell.run, extract the signing Team ID / designated requirement with `codesign -dv`, and require it to match the running bundle's own Team ID (fall back to warn-and-confirm while builds are ad-hoc signed; once a Developer ID exists per talkie-distribution-state, make it fail-closed with a pinned Team ID). (3) Document in release_dev.sh that the sha256 line is now load-bearing and must never be dropped from the notes on `gh release edit`.

title: Transcripts, memory graph, and meeting notes are written with default permissions; ~/Talkie Meetings is deliberately outside TCC and nothing sets 0600/0700
description: The app is unsandboxed (deliberate — sandbox breaks paste), so data-at-rest protection is purely POSIX. No file or directory anywhere in Sources ever sets posixPermissions (a repo-wide grep for setAttributes/posixPermissions/0o600/umask finds zero hits in Swift sources), so everything is created with the default umask: history.json with full transcripts (HistoryStore.swift:55 `data.write(to: fileURL, options: .atomic)`), the context graph, dictionary.json, context_summary.json, scratchpad — all in ~/Library/Application Support/Talkie — and every meeting transcript .md plus retained meeting AUDIO in ~/Talkie Meetings (Meeting.swift:554), a folder AppPaths.swift:15-17 explicitly places in the home root because it is 'NOT TCC-protected like ~/Documents'. On any Mac whose home directory predates Big Sur's 0700 default (upgraded accounts are 0755), every other local user can read the user's complete dictation history and meeting recordings. Even on 0700 homes, 0600 files are the stated bar in this audit's threat model and cost nothing.
evidence: /// ~/Talkie Meetings — a plain, user-accessible home folder (NOT TCC-protected like ~/Documents) so meeting transcripts are easy to point Claude at.
proposed_fix: In AppPaths.ensure(_:) (Sources/Talkie/AppPaths.swift:24-28), pass attributes [.posixPermissions: 0o700] to createDirectory (covers both supportDirectory() and meetingsDirectory(), and UpdaterPaths.updatesDir in Sources/TalkieUpdater/UpdaterSupport.swift:133 for the staged swap.sh). Add a small helper (e.g. in TalkieFileKit or next to FileShredder) `writeProtected(_ data: Data, to url: URL)` that does the atomic write then `try? FileManager.default.setAttributes([.posixPermissions: 0o600], ofItemAtPath: url.path)`, and route the sensitive writers through it: HistoryFileWriter.write (HistoryStore.swift:55), MeetingStore.writeMarkdown (Meeting.swift:554) and its index write (:676), ContextSummaryStore, ScratchpadStore, DictionaryStore, and the vector sidecar. Keep ~/Talkie Meetings where it is (the Claude-pointability is a product decision) — 0700 on the folder preserves that for the owner while closing it to other users.

title: Dictionary inbox applies mutations from ANY local process and attributes them all to 'Claude'; replacement rules can rewrite future dictated text
description: The inbox (~/Library/Application Support/Talkie/inbox/) is watched and auto-applies any well-formed JSON suggestion dropped there — there is no provenance check that the writer was the bundled talkie-mcp. The defenses are real (visible HUD pill with one-tap Undo, 40-char term cap, 5/min rate cap, kind/op validation, meeting retitle capped at 200 chars) and the design is deliberate (A5), but two gaps remain: (1) any process running as the user — an npm postinstall script, a malicious app, another agent — can inject a spoken→written replacement rule that from then on silently rewrites what the user dictates (e.g. rewriting a name, address, or URL every time it is spoken); a user who glances away for the ~few-second pill window has permanently accepted it, and the 5/min cap allows persistent retries until one lands unobserved; (2) the pill hard-codes the actor as Claude ('Claude added “%@” → “%@” to dictionary', DictionaryInbox.swift:303, similarly :281/:328/:346/:365/:390), so a hostile writer gets to impersonate the trusted brand in the consent UI.
evidence: presentPill(String(format: "Claude added “%@” → “%@” to dictionary".loc, from, to))
proposed_fix: Two proportionate hardenings that keep the A5 flow intact: (1) upgrade replacement-rule ADD/UPDATE ops (the text-rewriting ones) from apply-with-undo to confirm-before-apply — reuse the existing pill but make the primary action 'Add' instead of 'Undo', leaving vocabulary adds (recognition hints, low blast radius) on the current auto-apply path; (2) change the pill copy from 'Claude added…' to a neutral 'A suggestion was queued…' or verify provenance before claiming Claude: have talkie-mcp include its pid in the suggestion file and have DictionaryInbox check the writing process (or at minimum keep an audit trail of applied suggestions in the ActivityStore so an unnoticed rule is discoverable afterwards). Also surface active learned replacement rules prominently in the Dictionary view so an injected rewrite rule cannot hide.

title: Bulk 'Copy All' places the entire dictation history on the shared clipboard in one click
description: Adjacent to the Clear control being removed, the 'Copy All' header button (MemoryView.swift:89-94) copies history.allAsText() — every retained transcript — to NSPasteboard.general, where any clipboard manager, Universal Clipboard (which syncs to other Apple devices via iCloud), or clipboard-reading app picks it up. Listed here because the owner asked for an inventory of bulk controls; this is the only bulk-egress one. It is a legitimate feature, but its blast radius mirrors the Clear button's: one click moves the whole corpus off Talkie's protected storage.
evidence: Button { copyToClipboard(history.allAsText()) } label: { Label("Copy All", systemImage: "doc.on.doc") }
proposed_fix: Owner decision, not a required change. If kept, consider marking the pasteboard item transient/concealed so clipboard history tools skip it: in copyToClipboard (MemoryView.swift:283-287) use pb.setString under the org.nspasteboard.ConcealedType / TransientType marker types alongside .string, which well-behaved clipboard managers honor. Alternatively replace 'Copy All' with an export-to-file flow so the data lands in a user-chosen 0600 file instead of the shared pasteboard.

title: In-app dev updater de-quarantines and installs downloads with no code-signature check
description: Before swapping itself for the downloaded bundle, the updater verifies only (a) byte size from the GitHub API, (b) an optional SHA-256 parsed from the release notes body, and (c) the CFBundleIdentifier string — then strips quarantine so Gatekeeper never assesses the new code: `_ = Shell.run("/usr/bin/xattr", ["-dr", "com.apple.quarantine", newApp.path])`. Both the size and the sha256 line come from the same GitHub release the artifact does, so anyone who can publish a `dev-*` release (compromised gh auth, leaked PAT, repo collaborator) ships arbitrary code that inherits the recipient's mic/Accessibility/Input-Monitoring TCC grants. The digest protects only against transport corruption, not a malicious release. There is no `codesign --verify` and no Team-ID/anchor pin.
evidence: _ = Shell.run("/usr/bin/xattr", ["-dr", "com.apple.quarantine", newApp.path])
proposed_fix: In performInstall(), after unzip and before the xattr strip, run `codesign --verify --deep --strict <newApp>` and check the signing identity: `codesign -dv` (or SecStaticCodeCheckValidity with a requirement string `anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = "<TEAMID>"`). Refuse to de-quarantine/install unless the new bundle is validly signed by the expected Team ID (fall back to requiring signer == current bundle's signer for ad-hoc dev cases, with a loud UI warning). Keep the size+sha256 checks as-is; they become defense-in-depth instead of the sole gate.

title: Updater SHA-256 gate is fail-open when the release body omits a digest
description: verifyArtifact() enforces the digest only `if let expected = expectedSHA256?.lowercased()`. GitHubReleases.sha256(fromBody:) returns nil whenever no valid `sha256:` line exists (Sources/TalkieUpdater/GitHubReleases.swift:224-235), so a release published without the line — including a malicious one that simply omits it — installs on the size check alone. The comment frames this as backward compatibility for pre-digest releases, but it also gives any future publisher a one-line downgrade path.
evidence: if let expected = expectedSHA256?.lowercased() {
proposed_fix: Make the digest mandatory going forward: pick the first build number published with a digest (all dev-N releases since release_dev.sh started embedding it) and in verifyArtifact()/installAndRelaunch() reject any release with build >= that floor whose assetSHA256 is nil (`.badArtifact("release publishes no sha256 digest")`). Keep the nil-tolerant path only for builds below the floor, or drop it entirely if no pre-digest releases remain on the dev channel.

title: check-no-network.sh silently skips any .swift file whose path contains whitespace
description: The scan loop is `for f in $(grep -rl --include='*.swift' '' "${SCAN_DIRS[@]}" ...)` — an unquoted command substitution that word-splits paths. A file named e.g. `Sources/Talkie/Net Helper.swift` splits into two nonexistent paths; the awk invocation fails, and the trailing `|| true` on line 234 swallows the error. SwiftPM still compiles every .swift in the target directory regardless of name, so a whitespace-named file containing URLSession would ship while the repo's central zero-network gate (and the no-network.yml self-test, whose fixtures have no spaces) stays green. This is a confirmed bypass of the project's most important security control.
evidence: for f in $(grep -rl --include='*.swift' '' "${SCAN_DIRS[@]}" 2>/dev/null); do
proposed_fix: Iterate NUL-safely: `grep -rlZ --include='*.swift' '' "${SCAN_DIRS[@]}" | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do awk ... ; done` (or `find "${SCAN_DIRS[@]}" -name '*.swift' -print0 | xargs -0 ...`). Also drop the blanket `|| true` on the loop and instead fail loudly if awk cannot open a file. Add a fifth assertion to .github/workflows/no-network.yml that plants a fixture named 'Sources/Talkie/__ci self test__.swift' containing an https:// literal and asserts the gate rejects it.

title: Zero-network gate has no tier for process-spawn escapes (Process → /usr/bin/curl passes CI)
description: The HARD ban list covers only in-process network APIs (`urlsession|nsurlconnection|urlrequest|cfnetwork|...|getaddrinfo|socket(`). The scanned core already legitimately spawns subprocesses (e.g. Sources/Talkie/Permissions.swift:124 `let task = Process()`, DoctorReport.swift:169, RunShortcutIntent.swift:100), so code that shells out to `/usr/bin/curl`, `nscurl`, or `nc` would open a network connection while every gate stays green — the exact rot/malicious-PR scenario the gate exists to catch.
evidence: HARD  = "urlsession|nsurlconnection|urlrequest|cfnetwork|cfstream|cfsocket|nwconnection|nwlistener|network[.]framework|getaddrinfo|[^a-z_]socket[(]"
proposed_fix: Add a HARD substring tier for known network binaries (`/usr/bin/curl`, `curl `, `nscurl`, `/usr/bin/nc`, `wget`) and a SOFT tier for `Process(`/`executableURL`/`posix_spawn` excusable only via a new allow-listed marker reason (e.g. `// talkie:no-network(local-exec:<tool>)`) so every subprocess launch in the core is an audited, printed exception like the URL/Socket ones. Extend the no-network.yml self-test with a fixture that spawns curl and assert rejection.

title: GitHub Actions pinned by mutable tag (@v4), including the workflow that holds the Developer ID cert
description: All three workflows use `uses: actions/checkout@v4` (ci/release.yml:51, .github/workflows/ci.yml:58 and 125, .github/workflows/no-network.yml:44). A `v4` tag is mutable — a compromise of the actions/checkout repo can retarget it, and the release workflow runs with `permissions: contents: write` and secrets DEVELOPER_ID_CERT_P12 / APPLE_APP_PASSWORD in scope. The repo already applies the correct standard elsewhere: ci.yml sha256-pins the actionlint tarball (ACTIONLINT_SHA256, ci.yml:97) precisely so 'a tampered or swapped asset fails the build'. The same standard should apply to actions.
evidence: uses: actions/checkout@v4
proposed_fix: Pin every `uses:` to a full commit SHA with the tag as a trailing comment, e.g. `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2`, in ci/release.yml, .github/workflows/ci.yml (both jobs), and .github/workflows/no-network.yml. Optionally add Dependabot `github-actions` ecosystem config to keep the SHAs fresh.

title: Release pipeline is inert: ci/release.yml is not under .github/workflows/, though the cask says it is
description: GitHub Actions only executes workflows in .github/workflows/; the tag-driven release pipeline lives at ci/release.yml, so pushing a v* tag builds and signs nothing, and the cask placeholders (`version "0.0.0"`, `sha256 :no_check`) are never rewritten. Casks/talkie.rb line 16 tells users 'the release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) builds + notarizes Talkie.zip' — a path that does not exist. Related latent defects in the parked file: the Xcode-26 selection is silent-if-absent (`if [ -d /Applications/Xcode_26.app ]`, ci/release.yml:65 — a pattern ci.yml:128 explicitly calls out as wrong) and `runs-on: macos-15` (line 46) predates the macos-26 runner ci.yml already uses.
evidence: # workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) builds + notarizes Talkie.zip, uploads
proposed_fix: If the pipeline is deliberately parked until the Developer ID cert exists, add a top-of-file NOTE in ci/release.yml stating it is staged and must be moved to .github/workflows/release.yml to activate, and fix the Casks/talkie.rb:16 comment to point at ci/release.yml. When activating: move the file, change runs-on to macos-26, and replace the silent Xcode fallback with the hard-fail guard from ci.yml's 'Require Xcode 26' step.

title: .mcpb connector bundles an unsigned talkie-mcp binary inside the signed app
description: build_mcpb.sh zips the raw SwiftPM output (`cp "$BIN" "$STAGE/server/talkie-mcp"`) with no codesign step, and build_app.sh:139 embeds the resulting Talkie.mcpb in Contents/Resources of the app. The copy at Contents/MacOS/talkie-mcp IS signed (build_app.sh:262), but the second copy inside the zip is not. Claude Desktop extracts and executes that unsigned, quarantine-tainted binary — on a recipient's Mac (cask/notarized distribution) Gatekeeper can block it or it runs with no publisher identity, and an unsigned Mach-O inside a bundled archive is exactly the kind of thing a future notarization submission of the outer app can trip over.
evidence: cp "$BIN" "$STAGE/server/talkie-mcp"
proposed_fix: In scripts/build_mcpb.sh, after copying the binary into $STAGE/server/, sign it the same way build_app.sh signs the nested copy: `codesign --force --sign "${TALKIE_SIGN_ID:--}" --identifier com.coralate.talkie.mcp "$STAGE/server/talkie-mcp"`, adding `--options runtime --timestamp` when the identity is a Developer ID (mirror build_app.sh's NESTED_SIGN_ARGS branch; pass the identity through an env var so notarize.sh/build_app.sh can forward it).

title: .gitignore covers neither release zips nor the documented voice/benchmark corpora in the repo root
description: scripts/notarize.sh:20 writes `ZIP="$ROOT/Talkie.zip"` and release_dev.sh:40 creates `Talkie-dev-N.zip` in the repo root (deleted only on the success path — a failed `gh release` upload leaves it behind). Sources/TalkieBench/main.swift's HOW TO RUN tells the user to extract LibriSpeech into the working directory (`tar xzf test-clean.tar.gz # → LibriSpeech/test-clean/...`) and to build a self-recorded `./plosive-clips` corpus of their own voice. None of `*.zip`, `LibriSpeech/`, `test-clean.tar.gz`, or a corpus directory appears in .gitignore, so a `git add -A` in the canonical checkout can commit multi-GB corpora or the user's own voice recordings to the (eventually public) repo. The planned M0 jargon-corpus recording work raises the odds of exactly this.
evidence:
.build/
*.app
.DS_Store
proposed_fix: Append to .gitignore: `/Talkie.zip`, `/Talkie-*.zip`, `/LibriSpeech/`, `/test-clean.tar.gz`, `/plosive-clips/`, and a general `/corpus/` (or whatever directory the M0 jargon corpus lands in). Also consider `*.flac`/`*.wav` at repo root if no audio is ever meant to be committed.

title: 'Entitlements prove no network' claim overstates enforcement — the app is not sandboxed
description: The gate's PASS output tells users to verify with `codesign -d --entitlements - Talkie.app   # → no com.apple.security.network.client`, and scripts/install.sh:15-16 says the app 'stays provably zero-network (Resources/talkie.entitlements omits com.apple.security.network.client'. But `com.apple.security.network.client` is an App Sandbox entitlement, and Resources/talkie.entitlements contains no `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` key — the sandbox is (deliberately, it breaks paste injection) not enabled, so macOS enforces no network restriction from that omission at all. The grep gate and a live firewall check are the real evidence; the entitlement line implies an OS-level guarantee that does not exist. Do NOT enable the sandbox to fix this — fix the wording.
evidence: echo "  codesign -d --entitlements - Talkie.app   # → no com.apple.security.network.client"
proposed_fix: Reword the claim in check-no-network.sh's PASS footer (line 285-287) and scripts/install.sh:15-16 (and any matching text in docs/PRIVACY.md) to be accurate: the entitlements file shows Talkie requests no network capability, but since the app is not App-Sandboxed this is a transparency signal, not an OS-enforced block; the enforced guarantees are the CI source gate plus live verification (`nettop -p $(pgrep Talkie)` / Little Snitch).

title: Permissions.relaunch() interpolates the bundle path into a /bin/sh -c string
description: relaunch() builds a shell command by string interpolation: `task.arguments = ["-c", "sleep 0.4; open \"\(path)\""]` where path is Bundle.main.bundlePath. A bundle path containing `"`, backticks, or `$( )` (e.g. Talkie unzipped into a crafted folder name in ~/Downloads instead of /Applications) executes attacker-chosen shell. Practical exposure is low, but the shell hop is unnecessary — the updater's own swap script shows the project already knows to shQuote (UpdateInstaller.swift:155), and this call site predates that discipline.
evidence: task.arguments = ["-c", "sleep 0.4; open \"\(path)\""]
proposed_fix: Drop /bin/sh entirely: run `/usr/bin/open` directly with the path as an argv element (Process with executableURL=/usr/bin/open, arguments=[path]) after a Task.sleep, or use NSWorkspace.shared.openApplication(at:configuration:) from a detached helper — argv arrays never re-parse the path.

title: Documented install path is curl | sh with no integrity anchor
description: The canonical from-source install is `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/.../main/scripts/install.sh | sh` (also echoed to the user at line 81). The script itself is careful (set -eu, preflights, refuses dirty trees, ff-only pulls), but pipe-to-shell means the executed bytes are whatever `main` serves at that instant, unverifiable after the fact, and a truncated download can execute a partial script. For a privacy-marketed project whose thesis is 'grep it yourself', the install path is the one step that skips the grep.
evidence: #   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jannallenberger/Talkie/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
proposed_fix: Offer (and document first in docs/INSTALL.md) the two-step alternative: `git clone https://github.com/jannallenberger/Talkie && ~/Talkie/scripts/run.sh` — which is nearly what install.sh does anyway. Additionally wrap the script body in `main() { ... }; main "$@"` so a truncated pipe download executes nothing (the function never gets called unless fully received).

title: Tag-triggered release workflow pushes directly to main via checkout -B
description: The cask-bump step runs from the tag's detached HEAD and does `git checkout -B main` + `git push origin HEAD:main`. That local `main` points at the tag commit, so if origin/main has advanced past the tag the non-force push is rejected and the release run fails at its final step (asset published, cask stale); and structurally, any tag push becomes a write to the default branch under the workflow's `permissions: contents: write`. Combined with branch protection this step would always fail; without it, tag-pushers can effectively commit to main through CI.
evidence: git checkout -B main
proposed_fix: Replace with a fetch-and-rebase flow: `git fetch origin main && git checkout -B cask-bump origin/main`, commit the cask change there, and either push a branch + open a PR (`gh pr create --fill`) or, if direct commit is wanted, push the bump branch onto main only after `git pull --rebase origin main`. When the cask later moves to a homebrew-talkie tap repo (as the file's own comment anticipates), scope a fine-grained PAT to that repo only.

title: DictationAssembler is fully dead code — superseded by StreamingCleanup
description: The type `DictationAssembler` has zero references anywhere in Sources/ or Tests/ (grep for "DictationAssembler" matches only its own definition line). Its exact job — lock-guarded per-segment cleanup tasks started as segments finalize, joined in order at stop — is implemented, nearly line-for-line, by `StreamingCleanup` (Sources/Talkie/StreamingCleanup.swift), which is what AppDelegate actually wires up (`currentStreaming: StreamingCleanup?`, AppDelegate.swift:229). Both have the same NSLock + `[Task<String, Never>]` + `(await clean(trimmed)) ?? trimmed` fallback + `joined(separator: " ")` shape.
evidence: final class DictationAssembler: @unchecked Sendable {
proposed_fix: Delete Sources/Talkie/DictationAssembler.swift entirely (58 lines). No call sites exist, so nothing else changes. StreamingCleanup remains the single implementation.

title: PCM buffer conversion duplicated: TranscriptionEngine.OneShot/convertOne mirrors AudioCapture.SingleShotInput/convert
description: TranscriptionEngine carries a private `OneShot` class (line 601) and `convertOne` (line 634) that are byte-for-byte duplicates of AudioCapture's private `SingleShotInput` (AudioCapture.swift:7) and `convert` (AudioCapture.swift:364) — same capacity math (`ratio * frameLength + 1024`), same pull-block, same error handling. The comment on convertOne admits it: "Mirrors `AudioCapture.convert`." Two copies of realtime-sensitive conversion code will drift (e.g. the `primeMethod = .none` fix already had to be applied in both places).
evidence: /// Convert a single PCM buffer to `target`. Mirrors `AudioCapture.convert`.
proposed_fix: Extract one shared helper, e.g. a file-scope `enum AudioConversion { static func convert(_ buffer: AVAudioPCMBuffer, using converter: AVAudioConverter, to target: AVAudioFormat) -> AVAudioPCMBuffer? }` plus the one-shot input class, in a new small file (or in AudioCapture.swift as internal). Have AudioCapture's tap block, TranscriptionEngine.conform, and convertOne call it; delete `OneShot`, `convertOne`, and `SingleShotInput` (≈70 duplicated lines).

title: talkieDebugLog is a 'TEMPORARY' debug facility that became the app's logging system, writing transcript content to /tmp in production
description: The function's own doc says "TEMPORARY: remove once tuning is settled", yet it now has 84 call sites across 17 files (grep count) and unconditionally appends to /tmp/talkie-lang.log in every production run — including full dictation text (`cleanup[…]: in='…' out='…'` in CleanupEngine.swift:279, translations in OutputTranslator.swift:196). Besides the simplicity smell (a vestigial hack promoted to load-bearing infrastructure), it silently writes user speech to a world-readable temp file.
evidence: /// with `cat /tmp/talkie-lang.log`. TEMPORARY: remove once tuning is settled.
proposed_fix: Keep the single function but make it a no-op unless explicitly enabled: `guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["TALKIE_DEBUG_LOG"] != nil else { return }` (or a hidden Developer setting), and update the stale "TEMPORARY" comment to describe it as the opt-in diagnostics channel. No call sites change. Alternatively migrate to os.Logger with `.private` interpolation, but the env-gate is the S-sized fix.

title: TranscriptionEngine.transcribeBuffered has no callers — the meeting shim it served is gone
description: `transcribeBuffered(_:localeIdentifier:installIfNeeded:)` is documented as "used by the meeting language-correction shim", but that shim was removed; grep across Sources/ and Tests/ finds no call site — only the definition. Both remaining re-transcription consumers (MeetingRecorder.swift:1070, AppDelegate.swift:1604) call `transcribeCandidates` instead.
evidence:
func transcribeBuffered(
        _ buffers: [AVAudioPCMBuffer],
proposed_fix: Delete the `transcribeBuffered` method (lines 222–231, including its doc comment). `transcribeScored` and `transcribeCandidates` stay.

title: MeetingContextProvider protocol has no protocol-typed consumer; detectActiveMeeting() on the actor is dead and both conformers stub half the protocol
description: No code anywhere uses `any MeetingContextProvider` (grep: zero matches). Both call sites use concrete types (MeetingRecorder.swift:305 calls `CalendarMeetingContext().eventContext(at:)` directly; the detector's poll loop pushes via `onDetect`). Consequently: (a) `ActiveMeetingDetector.detectActiveMeeting()` (ActiveMeetingDetector.swift:316–323) has zero callers — verified dead; (b) `ActiveMeetingDetector.eventContext` (line 327) and `CalendarMeetingContext.detectActiveMeeting` (CalendarMeetingContext.swift:84) exist only as nil-returning stubs to satisfy a conformance nothing consumes. The protocol lumps two unrelated capabilities so each conformer must stub the other's.
evidence: protocol MeetingContextProvider: Sendable {
proposed_fix: Delete the dead `ActiveMeetingDetector.detectActiveMeeting()` method, both nil stubs, and the `: MeetingContextProvider` conformance clauses from ActiveMeetingDetector and CalendarMeetingContext. Either delete Protocols/MeetingContextProvider.swift or, if the roadmap seam should survive, split it into two one-method protocols (MeetingDetecting / MeetingEventContextProviding) and conform each type only to its own — but with no consumer, plain deletion is the honest simplification.

title: Notch-panel construction and positioning math exists in three copies (NotchPanel + two in HUD.swift)

title: MeetingRecorder.start() repeats the abort-teardown block three times

title: The "(imported: <filename>)" dedup marker is composed in three places

title: OutputTranslator.Decision is shared across two phases, producing unreachable switch arms

evidence:
case .accept, .fallback, nil:

proposed_fix: Change `preflight` to return `Bool` (`shouldSkipAsAlreadyTarget`) and drop `.skipAlreadyTarget` from `Decision`, leaving a two-case enum for decideOutput. `translate` becomes `if preflight(...) { return (text, false) }` and the unreachable arm disappears. title: HotKeyMonitor still documents the removed tap-tap-to-lock gesture; deferTimer comments describe behavior that no longer exists

description: TalkieMCP carries a 402-line byte-faithful copy of the app's semantic-search core (SemanticIndex.swift) guarded only by 20 grep-able MIRROR comments, plus Codable mirrors of Meeting/DictationEntry (TalkieStore.swift:197,221), a DictionarySuggestion shape mirrored against Sources/Talkie/DictionaryInbox.swift, and BrandMirror.swift. title: Ten stores hand-roll the identical JSON load/save persistence boilerplate
description: ActivityStore (251-260), AppUsageStore (142-151), LatencyStore (242-254), WordFrequencyStore (223-237), StatsStore (240-262), ScratchpadStore (154-165), MacroStore (66-75), AppProfileStore (108-119), NicheVocabStore (143-154), and ContextGraphStore (159-190) each reimplement the same pair: `guard let data = try? Data(contentsOf: fileURL), let decoded = try? JSONDecoder().decode(T.self, from: data) else { return }` and `guard let data = try? JSONEncoder().encode(x) else { return }; try? data.write(to: fileURL, options: .atomic)`. title: SRT/VTT/JSON renderers implemented twice (app vs CLI) with divergent cue-repair policies
description: Sources/Talkie/Export/TimedTranscriptRenderers.swift (TimedTranscriptExport: srt/vtt/csv/json + timecode clock + repaired()) and Sources/TalkieCLI/OutputFormats.swift (srt/vtt/json + srtTimestamp/vttTimestamp/clock + normalizedCues()) are parallel implementations of the same file formats. They have already diverged on cue hygiene: the app stretches degenerate cues to a 0.5 s floor (minimumCueSeconds = 0.5) while the CLI uses a 1 ms floor (let minEnd = start + 0.001), so the same recognizer output produces different subtitle files depending on which binary rendered it. The CLI already depends on TalkieFileKit, the designated shared home for exactly this kind of pure logic.
